front: Motion of a charge in a uniform electric field?
back: Constant force $qE$, constant acceleration $qE/m$ — along the field for +, against it for −.

front: Speed after accelerating from rest through p.d. V?
back: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = qV \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2qV/m}$

front: What is an electronvolt?
back: Energy gained by an electron crossing 1 V: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

front: Path of a charge entering a uniform E field at 90°?
back: A parabola — constant velocity along the plates, constant acceleration across them.

front: Magnetic force on a moving charge?
back: $F = qvB\sin\theta$, perpendicular to both v and B.

front: Why does a charge move in a circle in a uniform B field?
back: The force is always perpendicular to v: it does no work, so speed is constant and the force acts as a centripetal force.
concept: Circular motion in a magnetic field

front: Radius and period in a magnetic field?
back: $r = mv/qB$; $T = 2\pi m/qB$ (independent of speed).

front: Velocity selector condition?
back: $qE = qvB \Rightarrow v = E/B$, independent of q and m.

front: Force on a current-carrying wire?
back: $F = BIL\sin\theta$

front: Force per unit length between parallel wires?
back: $F/L = \mu_0I_1I_2/2\pi r$; same direction attract, opposite repel.

front: Force on charge $q$ between parallel plates with p.d. $V$ and separation $d$?
back: $F = qE = \dfrac{qV}{d}$ — the same everywhere between the plates.

front: Which way does an electron accelerate in an electric field?
back: Opposite to the field direction (towards the positive plate).

front: A particle crosses only part of the gap between plates. Which p.d. goes into $qV = \Delta E_k$?
back: The p.d. it actually moves through: $V \times \dfrac{\text{distance moved}}{d}$ for a uniform field.

front: An electron enters between plates of length $L$ with speed $v$ perpendicular to the field. How do you find its deflection?
back: Time in the field $t = L/v$ (horizontal speed constant). Vertical acceleration $a = eE/m$. Deflection $y = \tfrac12 at^2$.

front: A proton and an alpha particle are accelerated from rest through 100 V. Energy gained?
back: Proton: 100 eV. Alpha (charge $2e$): 200 eV $= 3.2\times10^{-17}$ J.

front: Define the **tesla**.
back: The flux density in which a 1 m wire carrying 1 A perpendicular to the field experiences a force of 1 N: 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹.

front: Can a magnetic field speed up a charged particle?
back: No. The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work: speed and kinetic energy stay constant, only the direction changes.

front: What force acts on a charge moving parallel to a magnetic field?
back: None: $F = qvB\sin 0^\circ = 0$.

front: How do you find the direction of the magnetic force on a moving charge?
back: Use Fleming’s left-hand rule (or a right-hand palm rule) with the current direction = direction of motion for a **positive** charge; reverse it for a negative charge.

front: Derive the radius of a charged particle’s circular path in a uniform B field.
back: Magnetic force = centripetal force: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

front: Why is the period of circular motion in a B field independent of speed?
back: $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$: a faster particle moves in a proportionally larger circle, so the time per orbit is the same.

front: Particles with the same speed enter a uniform B field. What makes their paths curve more tightly?
back: A smaller $m/q$, since $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$. This is the principle of separating isotopes by mass (mass spectrometry).

front: In a velocity selector, what happens to particles faster than $E/B$?
back: The magnetic force $qvB$ exceeds the electric force $qE$, so they are deflected towards the magnetic-force side. Slower particles deflect the other way.

front: What is the **motor effect**?
back: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, $F = BIL\sin\theta$, perpendicular to both the current and the field.

front: What is $L$ in $F = BIL\sin\theta$?
back: The length of wire **inside** the field, not the whole wire.

front: Two parallel wires carry current in the same direction. Attract or repel?
back: **Attract** (opposite directions repel) — the opposite of the rule for like charges.

front: Value and unit of $\mu_0$?
back: $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T m A⁻¹ (N A⁻²), the permeability of free space.
